coherence.reasons: Both follow the same sound hierarchy: market grows but is unprofitable, unit economics are negative, runway rule is broken, software is the alternative. Y's hierarchy is tighter. Its unit-economics claim rests on one fully loaded measure (contribution after store costs) applied to all four cases: plan +2.02, best observed -1.76, median -6.17, pop-up -12.57. Each section claim is then supported on that same basis, and the pop-up has its own section linking promotions, retention and acquisition cost. X's headline measure is contribution before store costs (-2.67). Its comparison table therefore shows the best-site case at +$0.5 under a section claim that Parcelbird Now 'would lose money per order', and the after-store-cost loss appears only as a sub-bullet and in the per-store slide. X's runway claim 'even on the founders' numbers' is also partly supported by a median-economics figure, which mixes two arguments. X's software section is internally consistent and its qualifier ('if sales outgrow today's pipeline') carries through to the title and assumptions.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred conclusion (do not launch, back the software), reject the nine-store plan and consider a one-store test. X weighs the alternatives more substantively. It costs a one-store pilot with Zipcart-style fees at about $2.43M (capex, store loss and acquisition) and shows it only just keeps the runway floor and competes with customers. It also tests the recommended option against the investors' actual objective, a path to profitability within current cash: breakeven ARR of $11.0M, reached in 2029 at 60% growth using about $6.6M, with a 40% growth sensitivity and an honest caveat that about 72 new contracts are needed, twice today's pipeline. Y's software case is thinner: about 10 contracts pay for the hires and runway falls only from 30 to 26 months, with no path to profitability shown. Y rejects the test store using median economics without the fee lever, so it does not weigh the most plausible version of a test. Y's three revisit conditions are clear and useful, and X has a comparable reopen test. X gives the board a better-weighed set of options.

evidence.reasons: Y reproduces the key's critical calculations exactly: median -6.17, best inputs observed -1.76, pop-up -12.57, plan +2.02, all after store costs. It correctly infers that the best-of-each-input case bounds all 14 sites, so no observed site makes money. Its supporting numbers check out: break-even order value of $46.7 before store costs and about $63 after, the pop-up loss bridge with promotions at 47.4%, nine-store results of -$18.2M, -$8M and +$12M, payback of 14.8 months, and runway of 6.2 months. X's arithmetic is also correct, and it adds valuable calculations Y lacks: the Zipcart-fee scenario on a median order ($3.02 before store costs, 1,043 orders a day to cover the store, matching the key's -$0.48 logic) and the acquisition cost to fill stores ($1.53M per store, $27.5M for the plan). But X never gives the best-observed case after store costs, showing it as +$0.5, and gives the pop-up only before store costs (-6.2), which understates two critical findings. It labels the pilot's $0.30M loss 'at median volume' when that figure is for volume 14% lower. Its software projection holds costs flat while ARR quadruples, which is flagged but strong. Y's weak spot is dismissing the Zipcart fee route by assertion ('cannot copy') rather than testing it.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis while conceding that the market growth is real, and both note that the pop-up's 18% weekly growth was bought with 12% promotions. Y refutes the 'density will fix it' claim more directly: even the best observed density combined with the best order value loses $1.76 after store costs, and the plan needs all four inputs beyond any site. X leaves that case at +$0.5 before store costs and makes the point through per-store losses instead. X handles the evidence that partly supports the founders more appropriately. It tests what happens if Parcelbird adopted Zipcart's fee and promotion cut, and finds a median order would pay per order but the store would need about 1,043 orders a day after a 14% volume loss. It then sets its reopen test on that basis. Y only says the plan does not charge the fee and so cannot copy the route, which does not test the adjusted hypothesis. Each is stronger on one half of the expected handling, so the difference is negligible.

overall.reasons: Both documents give the board a defensible 'do not launch, scale the software' answer with the runway breach shown correctly. Y serves the core decision somewhat better. It puts the decisive facts in fully loaded terms the board can act on: every observed case loses money after store costs (-6.17 median, -1.76 at the best inputs, -12.57 in the pop-up), and only the plan's beyond-range inputs turn positive. That is the cleanest answer to the founders' density argument, and it comes with clear revisit conditions. X is stronger on what to do instead and on the Zipcart nuance: the fee scenario, the pilot costing, and the software path to breakeven within cash, which speaks to the investors' objective. But X's reliance on before-store-cost contribution blunts its central economic case and leaves the best-site case looking marginally positive. On the critical insights, Y is ahead on three (median/best-case economics, the plan's inputs, the pop-up) and X on one (the fee evidence), so Y wins narrowly.
